title: Beathag gives up the list of the slab's turns
summary: Beathag, who has kept the household order of the slab's night watch eleven years, says at the Samhain gathering that she will keep the list no longer, after a household comes two nights running to a turn already missed. Thirty-one households now stand on it, too many for one memory to hold true.

title: The families agree to choose the slab's keeper by lot
summary: At the slab's own clearing the families of Tobar dhìreach and the near valleys meet to settle the watch. An old man of the gathering proposes a single keeper chosen by lot, to hold the slab until death or infirmity, rather than turns by household. No vote is taken; the silence that follows is read as agreement.

title: The lot falls to Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill
summary: At the next full dark, thirty-one households send one member each to draw from a bag of thirty pebbles and one marked white. The lot falls to Oighrig, a herder's daughter of three-and-thirty, who carries the marked stone in her belt from that night for the rest of her life.

title: Oighrig's father speaks of the shared name
summary: Walking home from the drawing, Oighrig's father Dòmhnall, a herder of the near slopes with no kinship to Rìghrean na Cloiche, tells her she will spend the rest of her keeping answering travellers who mistake her for blood of Dòmhnall Clachach, the second of that name to hold the north.

title: Taigh na Lice raised at Tobar dhìreach
summary: The families of the near valleys build Oighrig a house on the clearing's edge above the slab, its door set to face the stone and no other way, the first building on Dia-thìr raised for no reason but to stand near the vein.

title: Oighrig sits her first winter alone by the slab
summary: Moved into the new house at the first hard frost, Oighrig finds the keeper's long unbroken watch harder than any turn shared with her own household, and begins to notice things about the stain and the stone's temper that a thousand years of turned watches had never set down.

title: Oighrig comes to Niocol Snaidhear with her cupped hand
summary: In her third year of keeping, Oighrig goes to the stone-worker Niocol Snaidhear and sets her own hand on his bench, cupped as for water, asking for a cup of grey stone that will hold exactly what it holds, so that no household's handful of coal runs bigger than another's by the accident of whose palm measures it.

title: The first two stone cups crack in the grinding
summary: Niocol Snaidhear loses a first cup to a hidden vein in the stone and a second to a hair-crack struck too hard near its finishing, and keeps the flawed second on his bench through the grinding of the third as a thing to learn the shape of a mistake by.

title: Niocol finishes the cup ground to Oighrig's hand
summary: After eleven sittings across two summers, Niocol Snaidhear finishes a cup of grey stone fitted to Oighrig's hand, veined faintly white, holding exactly what her two cupped hands together cannot quite hold. She says the hand it copies is not her own but the hand of every hearth; Niocol begins a second cup as a copy before he is asked.

title: Word of the stone cup travels the near valleys
summary: News of Oighrig's cup and the trouble it answers reaches stone-workers at three other places within the year: a woman at Àth gharbh, an old man at Achadh dhìreach, and a household at Cnoc chaol, each asking to grind a copy against it.

title: Oighrig carries the first cup to Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol
summary: Oighrig walks the near valleys over a year with the first cup wrapped in wool, testing each new copy against it by pouring water from one to the other on a flat stone, and sending two cups at Achadh dhìreach and one at Cnoc chaol back to the wheel when the levels do not match.

title: The four cups are ground true at Àth gharbh, Achadh dhìreach and Cnoc chaol
summary: The copies of the stone cup are finished: quickest at Àth gharbh, where the worker measures against Niocol's cup throughout rather than a hand alone; slowest at Achadh dhìreach, an old man's hands steadied by his grandson through the last evenings; and, despite two false starts, fastest of all begun at Cnoc chaol.

title: Coinneachadh nan Cupan on the moor
summary: At a nameless spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, chosen because it lies equal walking from all four places and belongs to no one household, the four keepers of the cups fill each from the same water on a flat stone and pass every cup down the line for each hand to weigh. The water stands level in all four; the place is called from that morning Coinneachadh nan Cupan.

title: The hills measure the coal with one measure
summary: From the year of Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the households from the slopes above Tobar dhìreach to the poor ground of Cnoc chaol measure their handful of the vein's coal by the one cup and its three copies, and not by the hand that happens to do the measuring, a change the reciters afterward give no more than a single line.
